title: TypedInk: Knowing When Not To Draw
summary: Can a scientific figure generator know when it does not have enough evidence to draw? Complete-source illustrators map a finished methodology section to a schematic, or a table to plotting code, and are never asked this question because their input is assumed complete. The research record is rarely that complete: an outline, a draft paragraph, a table, or a one-sentence intent, in any combination, and painting measured numbers with an image model when the table is missing is a hallucinated result. TypedInk infers a figure type from {diagram, plot, plate} from a possibly incomplete source and dispatches to the renderer that can honor that type's evidence contract, refusing dispatch when the contract cannot be met. On the six gold plots in TypedFigBench (5 views, n=30), TypedInk's code path inks every gold table token when a table is observed (12/12), refuses the 12 hidden-table views instead of inventing numbers, and marks 6 intent-only views illustrative, with no execution failures. An always-draw coder with no such gate inks 30/30 charts, including all 18 with no table, and recovers zero gold numbers on any of them; two vision-language raters (not humans; human replication is future work) still judge those always-draw charts submittable 17/36 times, against TypedInk's refusal 0/36 times. A diagnostic field ablation of the type router (16 illustrations, 5 views each, n=80) locates where this failure would originate if unchecked: an outline alone yields type accuracy 0.31 and sends every gold plot into an integrity violation, and a chat-model planner narrows but does not close the gap (overall accuracy 0.85, still integrity-failing on 25% of outlines). Diagram-label recall is 0.47 on the full record and 0.19 on an outline. Gold plates are typed at dispatch (oracle integrity-fail 0.00) and rendered as stills.

AI.tldr: TypedInk is an evidence-aware scientific figure generator that selects diagram, plot, or plate rendering only when the available source supports that figure type; otherwise, it refuses or labels the output illustrative. On TypedFigBench, it reproduced all observed table tokens, refused to fabricate hidden-table plots, and avoided the integrity failures of an always-draw baseline.
AI.motivation: Scientific figure generators often assume complete methodological inputs, but real research records may contain only partial outlines, draft text, tables, or intentions. Generating measured plots without observed data can create hallucinated scientific results. The paper therefore addresses whether a figure generator can recognize insufficient evidence and abstain from rendering unsupported figures.
AI.method: TypedInk first infers a figure type—diagram, plot, or plate—from potentially incomplete source material. It then dispatches the request to a renderer governed by an evidence contract for that type. The system refuses dispatch when the contract cannot be satisfied and marks intent-only outputs as illustrative. Evaluation uses TypedFigBench, including six gold plots across five views with n=30, comparisons against an always-draw coder, two vision-language raters, and a diagnostic ablation of the type router using 16 illustrations across five views with n=80. The study also reports diagram-label recall and oracle integrity for gold plates.
AI.result: When a table was observed, TypedInk preserved every gold table token (12/12); for 12 hidden-table views, it refused to draw rather than invent numbers; and it marked six intent-only views as illustrative, with no execution failures. The always-draw baseline produced 30/30 charts, including all 18 without tables, but recovered zero gold numbers from them. Vision-language raters judged the baseline charts submittable 17/36 times, while TypedInk received 0/36 because it refused unsupported cases. Router ablations showed outline-only type accuracy of 0.31, causing every gold plot to violate integrity, while a chat-model planner reached 0.85 overall accuracy but still failed integrity on 25% of outlines. Diagram-label recall was 0.47 for the full record and 0.19 for outlines. Gold plates were typed at dispatch with oracle integrity failure of 0.00 and rendered as stills.
AI.conclusion: The results support evidence-gated figure generation as a safer alternative to unconditional chart production. TypedInk effectively prevents fabricated numeric plots when source evidence is missing and distinguishes illustrative intent from measured results. However, incomplete inputs remain difficult for type routing and diagram-label extraction, and the evaluation relies on vision-language raters rather than human judges; broader human replication and stronger routing methods are needed.

title: Designing UIs with GenAI: Understanding the Use, Benefits, and Limitations of Prompt-to-Design Generators
summary: The integration of generative AI (GenAI) into user interface (UI) design has led to prompt-to-design generators (P2dGens), tools that enable designers to create UI prototypes from textual prompts efficiently. Despite their growing adoption, little is known about how designers use these tools in everyday practice, their benefits, and limitations. We conducted semi-structured interviews with 17 UI designers to investigate P2dGens use, focusing on workflow integration, attitudes toward generator-assisted design, and the organizational climate. Findings show that designers primarily use P2dGens as ideation accelerators rather than end-to-end solutions, and they adopt a variety of individual and collaborative prompting strategies. Designers expressed complex attitudes, noting gains in efficiency and inspiration while also highlighting concerns about loss of personal creativity and design quality. We also observed emerging governance practices and varying attitudes within organizations toward P2dGens. These insights illuminate how P2dGens reshape UI design workflows and contribute to understanding human-AI collaboration in UI design.

AI.tldr: This study examines how 17 UI designers use prompt-to-design generators (P2dGens) in practice. It finds that designers mainly use them to accelerate ideation, not to produce complete designs, while balancing efficiency and inspiration against concerns about creativity, quality, and organizational governance.
AI.motivation: Although prompt-to-design generators are increasingly adopted for UI design, their use in everyday professional workflows, perceived benefits and limitations, prompting practices, and organizational contexts remain insufficiently understood. The study addresses this gap by investigating designers’ experiences and attitudes toward generator-assisted design.
AI.method: The researchers conducted semi-structured interviews with 17 UI designers. The interviews focused on how P2dGens are integrated into workflows, how designers perceive AI-assisted design, what individual and collaborative prompting strategies they use, and how organizational climates shape adoption and governance.
AI.result: Designers primarily use P2dGens as ideation accelerators rather than end-to-end design solutions. They employ diverse individual and collaborative prompting strategies. Reported benefits include improved efficiency and inspiration, while concerns include reduced personal creativity and compromised design quality. Organizations show differing attitudes toward adoption, alongside emerging governance practices.
AI.conclusion: P2dGens are reshaping UI design workflows and human-AI collaboration by supporting early-stage ideation rather than replacing designers’ complete processes. Their effective use depends on designers’ prompting practices, critical evaluation of generated outputs, and organizational norms and governance.

title: Project Progress Desk: Know Where All Your Claude Code and Codex Projects Stand at a Glance
comment: 6 pages, 4 figures. Submitted to IUI 2027 Demos
summary: Codex and Claude Code let developers work on many projects in parallel, but keeping track of them still means switching between chats, terminal sessions and providers. We present Project Progress Desk, a local desktop interface that brings overall progress, blockers and pending decisions into one view. Users can see which projects need attention, inspect what remains, and compare earlier approaches before choosing how to continue. Agent receipts link reported outcomes to each project's weighted acceptance checklist; the overview distinguishes receipt-supported progress from dated estimates. We describe daily use across 36 projects, including a choice between two implementations based on their recorded outcomes. At the demo, attendees will explore 30 simulated projects, trace completed work to overall progress, and watch a coding agent's new result update the overview.

AI.tldr: Project Progress Desk is a local desktop dashboard for monitoring multiple coding-agent projects. It consolidates progress, blockers, pending decisions, historical approaches, and evidence-backed acceptance status, and is demonstrated through real daily use across 36 projects plus 30 simulated projects.
AI.motivation: Developers using Codex, Claude Code, and similar tools must switch among chats, terminal sessions, and providers to understand the state of multiple projects. This fragmentation makes it difficult to identify which projects need attention, verify reported progress, and make informed decisions between alternative implementations.
AI.method: The paper presents a local desktop interface that provides a unified project overview. It tracks blockers and pending decisions, allows inspection of remaining work and comparison of prior approaches, and links agent receipts to weighted acceptance checklists. The interface explicitly separates receipt-supported progress from dated estimates. The system is evaluated through daily use across 36 projects, including a documented implementation choice based on recorded outcomes, and a demonstration with 30 simulated projects and live agent-result updates.
AI.result: The system supports centralized monitoring of many projects, traceability from reported outcomes to acceptance criteria, distinction between verified progress and estimates, and comparison of alternative implementations. The abstract reports practical use across 36 projects and a demonstration scenario involving 30 simulated projects, but does not provide quantitative usability, accuracy, or efficiency metrics.
AI.conclusion: Project Progress Desk offers an evidence-oriented way to manage parallel coding-agent work by combining project status, decision context, and acceptance-checklist traceability in one local interface. Its main contribution is improved visibility and accountability across projects, though stronger empirical evaluation is needed to establish benefits over existing workflows.

title: Ender: Visual Scaffolding for Geometric Proof Comprehension
summary: Geometric proof is a foundational but notoriously difficult topic in secondary mathematics, primarily due to the high cognitive load required to integrate visual diagrams with logical text. As proofs evolve, tracking the initial givens and an expanding set of derived truths can easily overwhelm working memory. While established scaffolding techniques are often visual and diagram-based, current digital learning environments mostly rely on static, text-heavy interfaces that force students to manage these complex mental models on their own. This paper introduces Ender, an interactive rendering system designed to visualize the logical status of two-column proofs. Ender's design is grounded in four literature-derived requirements: (1) diagram annotation, (2) structural tracing, (3) support for partial or incorrect work, and (4) synchronization between the diagram and text. To evaluate the system, we conducted a between-subjects, think-aloud experiment with 12 secondary school students in the United States, comparing Ender against a traditional digital proof interface. Our results indicate that students using Ender performed significantly better on proof comprehension tasks--specifically in identifying and correcting logical errors. These findings suggest that dynamic visual scaffolding may ease the working memory burden of digital interfaces, offering a promising building block for future AI-based proof tutoring systems.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Ender, an interactive system that visually represents the logical status of two-column geometric proofs. In a controlled study with 12 U.S. secondary students, Ender improved proof comprehension, particularly students’ ability to identify and correct logical errors, compared with a conventional digital interface.
AI.motivation: Geometric proof is difficult because students must coordinate visual diagrams, formal text, givens, and accumulated deductions while managing substantial working-memory demands. Existing digital proof tools are largely static and text-heavy, providing limited support for maintaining these interconnected representations. The paper therefore seeks to develop visual scaffolding that makes proof structure and logical status more explicit.
AI.method: The authors designed Ender around four requirements derived from prior literature: diagram annotation, structural tracing, support for partial or incorrect proof work, and synchronization between diagrams and proof text. They evaluated it through a between-subjects think-aloud experiment involving 12 secondary school students in the United States. Students used either Ender or a traditional digital proof interface and completed proof-comprehension tasks.
AI.result: Students using Ender performed significantly better on proof-comprehension tasks, especially identifying and correcting logical errors. The findings suggest that dynamic visual scaffolding can reduce the cognitive burden associated with coordinating diagrams and textual proof structures.
AI.conclusion: Ender demonstrates the potential of synchronized, interactive visual support for learning geometric proof. The system may serve as a foundation for future AI-based proof tutoring systems, although the small sample and limited evaluation context warrant further investigation with larger and more diverse populations and additional learning measures.

title: Designing Accessible and Rigorous ML Experiments: No-Code Visual Workflows and Structured Guidance for Beginners
summary: Designing machine learning (ML) experiments requires beginners to plan a methodologically sound workflow and implement it in a concrete environment. We evaluated two forms of support in two within-participant studies with 18 predominantly technically trained participants: mlguide, which provides structured, evidence- backed guidance for workflow design, and AI Sandbox, a visual no-code environment for workflow implementation. After using mlguide, participants produced better high-level workflow designs, but their scores on a quiz about specific methodological choices did not improve significantly. Compared with Google Colab, AI Sandbox received higher hedonic user experience ratings, while perceived workload and acceptance did not differ significantly. These findings suggest that different forms of interactive support help with differ- ent aspects of beginner ML experimentation. The paper contributes a reusable evaluation task with instructions, a modified dataset, and a quiz, as well as empirical evidence on structured guidance for workflow design and on the experience of implementing workflows in visual and notebook-based environments.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates two complementary supports for beginners conducting machine-learning experiments: mlguide for planning sound workflows and AI Sandbox for implementing them in a visual no-code environment. Across two within-participant studies with 18 mainly technically trained participants, mlguide improved the quality of high-level workflow designs, but did not significantly improve knowledge of specific methodological choices. AI Sandbox was rated as providing a more enjoyable user experience than Google Colab, although workload and acceptance were comparable. The work contributes an evaluation protocol, modified dataset, quiz, and empirical findings about beginner ML support.
AI.motivation: Beginners often struggle with both the methodological planning and practical implementation of ML experiments. Existing support may address only one of these challenges, so the paper investigates whether structured evidence-based guidance and a visual no-code environment can improve different aspects of the workflow.
AI.method: The authors conducted two within-participant studies involving 18 predominantly technically trained participants. They evaluated mlguide, a structured guidance tool for designing ML workflows, and AI Sandbox, a visual no-code environment for implementing workflows. Participants' workflow designs, quiz performance on methodological decisions, user experience, perceived workload, and acceptance were compared with relevant baselines, including Google Colab.
AI.result: mlguide led to better high-level workflow designs, but the improvement in quiz scores for specific methodological choices was not statistically significant. AI Sandbox received higher hedonic user-experience ratings than Google Colab. No significant differences were found in perceived workload or acceptance.
AI.conclusion: Interactive support should be designed according to the particular stage of ML experimentation it targets: structured guidance can improve overall workflow planning, while visual environments can make implementation more enjoyable. However, neither intervention clearly improved all aspects of methodological understanding or usability. The paper also offers reusable materials for future evaluation research.

title: Towards Accessible, Autonomous Photosynthesis Monitoring on Living Leaves
summary: Photosynthesis is a direct biomarker of plant health and functioning. However, measuring net photosynthesis on individual leaves requires expensive (USD 42,000 - USD 89,000) instruments and manual effort. This limits access to photosynthesis sensing and makes long-term monitoring across multiple leaves difficult. We present a 1000x low-cost, autonomous sensing system that enables longitudinal monitoring of photosynthesis on living leaves over multiple days. Guided by a formative user study with 13 plant biology researchers, the system integrates an automated, leaf-attached chamber with a low-cost CO2 sensor. Built using a 3D-printed clamp and thermoformed dome, the chamber periodically closes to measure CO2 drawdown and reopens to refresh the air. Each chamber costs about USD 62 and operates independently, allowing multiple leaves to be monitored simultaneously without pumps or gas tubing. We characterize each chamber and validate its measurements against a research-grade gas exchange instrument (CIRAS-4) across 29 sessions (R^2 = 0.90). We also demonstrate monitoring of C3 and CAM photosynthesis plants, adaptability to different leaf geometries, and a light-response experiment. In a nine-day deployment, six chambers captured simultaneous CO2 exchange from individual leaves of the same plant during drought and rewatering. Each leaf showed different patterns of nighttime CO2 uptake and recovery, which a whole-plant CO2 measurement instrument would obscure. To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration of such leaf-level photosynthesis dynamics using independent, low-cost autonomous chambers. Our work opens new opportunities for plant science, education, and data-driven agriculture.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a low-cost, autonomous leaf-attached system for measuring photosynthetic CO2 exchange over multiple days. It reduces the cost of individual-leaf monitoring by roughly 1000-fold compared with conventional instruments and achieves strong agreement with a research-grade system (R² = 0.90).
AI.motivation: Photosynthesis is an important indicator of plant health, but conventional leaf-level gas-exchange instruments are expensive, require manual operation, and are poorly suited to long-term, simultaneous monitoring of multiple leaves. These limitations prevent detailed observation of leaf-to-leaf variation, especially under changing conditions such as drought and rewatering.
AI.method: The authors conducted a formative study with 13 plant biology researchers and designed an autonomous leaf-attached chamber consisting of a 3D-printed clamp, thermoformed dome, and low-cost CO2 sensor. The chamber periodically seals around a living leaf to measure CO2 drawdown, then reopens to refresh the air. Independent chambers operate without pumps or gas tubing, enabling simultaneous measurements. The system was characterized and validated against a CIRAS-4 research-grade gas-exchange instrument across 29 sessions, and tested on C3 and CAM plants, different leaf geometries, light-response conditions, and a nine-day drought-and-rewatering deployment involving six leaves.
AI.result: Each chamber costs approximately USD 62, compared with USD 42,000–89,000 for conventional instruments. Measurements correlated strongly with the CIRAS-4 (R² = 0.90). The system successfully measured photosynthetic behavior in both C3 and CAM plants, accommodated varied leaf geometries, captured light responses, and operated autonomously for nine days. During drought and recovery, leaves on the same plant displayed distinct nighttime CO2 uptake and recovery patterns that whole-plant measurements would have masked.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates a substantially cheaper, scalable, and autonomous approach to longitudinal, leaf-level photosynthesis monitoring. Its independent operation and low cost enable multi-leaf experiments that reveal spatial and temporal variation within plants, with potential applications in plant science, education, and data-driven agriculture. The evidence supports feasibility and measurement validity, although broader validation across species, environments, and longer deployments would strengthen the claims.

title: EJAI: Judgment-Preserving Civic AI for Data Center Environmental Justice
summary: Communities in the United States and around the world are contesting data centers, the physical infrastructure of AI. These disputes pose environmental justice issues: residents must weigh unevenly distributed burdens using evidence scattered across metrics, corporate claims, policy documents, and public testimony. A formative study with 10 users showed that dashboards and single-agent AI can settle questions before people examine that evidence. Here we present EJAI, a source-grounded system that links an interactive map, retrieved evidence, missing-data statements, and two stakeholder personas that allow people to inspect evidence and form their own policy recommendations. In a small functional benchmark of 21 queries, retrieved evidence supported 98.4% of factual claims and the system acknowledged missing evidence in 32 of 33 cases. Persona alignment carried a grounding cost: the Corporate Executive omitted some evidence that conflicted with its assigned priorities. In a within-subjects study, 15 participants acting as residents prepared for a simulated town hall. Some checked cited AI claims while treating map metrics as official, some made conditional recommendations with safeguards such as water-use disclosure, and some found the personas simplified or biased. Our results suggest that civic AI can support preparation for public reasoning when it makes evidence, gaps, and disagreement open to inspection, and that corpus imbalance and two-sided personas remain open justice concerns.

AI.tldr: EJAI is a source-grounded civic AI system designed to help communities examine evidence about data-center impacts and develop their own policy recommendations. It combines an interactive map, retrieved sources, explicit missing-data statements, and two stakeholder personas. A benchmark and user study suggest strong factual grounding and useful support for public-reasoning preparation, while revealing risks from persona bias, corpus imbalance, and overtrust in map metrics.
AI.motivation: Communities are increasingly required to evaluate the environmental and distributive impacts of data centers, but relevant evidence is fragmented across quantitative metrics, corporate statements, policy documents, and public testimony. The authors are motivated by concerns that dashboards and conventional single-agent AI may prematurely resolve contested questions, preventing users from inspecting evidence, recognizing uncertainty, and forming independent judgments. The paper therefore addresses how civic AI can support environmental-justice reasoning without obscuring disagreement or missing data.
AI.method: The authors present EJAI, a source-grounded system integrating an interactive map, retrieved evidence, explicit statements about missing information, and two stakeholder personas representing different priorities. They evaluate it in three ways: (1) a formative study with 10 users examining how dashboards and single-agent AI affect evidence engagement; (2) a functional benchmark of 21 queries assessing factual support and acknowledgment of missing evidence; and (3) a within-subjects study with 15 participants acting as residents preparing for a simulated town hall. The study observes evidence checking, recommendation formation, use of safeguards, and perceptions of persona simplification or bias.
AI.result: In the functional benchmark, retrieved evidence supported 98.4% of factual claims, and the system acknowledged missing evidence in 32 of 33 cases. However, persona alignment introduced a grounding trade-off: the Corporate Executive persona omitted some evidence conflicting with its assigned priorities. In the user study, participants varied in how they interacted with the system: some verified cited AI claims but treated map metrics as authoritative, some developed conditional recommendations incorporating safeguards such as water-use disclosure, and some viewed the personas as simplistic or biased.
AI.conclusion: EJAI can help people prepare for civic deliberation when evidence, uncertainty, missing information, and disagreement remain inspectable rather than being collapsed into a single answer. The findings support source-grounded, transparency-oriented civic AI, but also identify unresolved justice concerns: uneven source coverage may reproduce corpus imbalance, and stakeholder personas may simplify or bias contested perspectives. The system should therefore be understood as an aid to public reasoning, not an authoritative decision-maker.

title: EyeQ: Exploring Corneal Reflection for Mobile Context Sensing
summary: What if a single face-facing camera could sense your surroundings---through your eyes? We introduce EyeQ, which explores corneal reflection as a modality for context-aware mobile interaction. Traditional vision-based context sensing relies on world-facing cameras that demand explicit aiming or dual-camera setups; EyeQ instead shows that an off-the-shelf VLM can read scene context from corneal reflections captured with a smartphone camera. To recover usable detail from mobile corneal crops, EyeQ pairs on-device iris-guided capture with server-side AI enhancement, then leverages VLMs to extract scene types, names, and objects from warped, unfamiliar eye-image sequences. In an N=10 study, we characterize how capture conditions shape reflection fidelity, evaluate what VLMs detect, misclassify, and hallucinate, and demonstrate interaction opportunities, including detecting a steering wheel to distinguish drivers from passengers. This work reframes the eye in HCI---from a target for gaze estimation to a passive mirror of one's surroundings---and examines the privacy tensions it raises.

AI.tldr: EyeQ presents a corneal-reflection sensing system that uses a smartphone’s face-facing camera, iris-guided capture, AI enhancement, and vision-language models (VLMs) to infer surrounding scene context without a dedicated world-facing camera. A small N=10 study evaluates capture conditions, VLM recognition errors, hallucinations, and interaction use cases such as distinguishing drivers from passengers.
AI.motivation: Existing mobile context sensing commonly depends on world-facing cameras, which require deliberate aiming, or on dual-camera hardware. EyeQ investigates whether corneal reflections can serve as a passive optical proxy for the user’s surroundings, potentially enabling context-aware interaction through a single front-facing camera. The work is also motivated by reframing the eye as a source of environmental information while examining the resulting privacy implications.
AI.method: The system captures corneal reflections using a smartphone’s front-facing camera, with iris-guided on-device capture to obtain usable eye-image crops. Server-side AI enhancement attempts to restore detail from the small, warped, and unfamiliar reflection images. VLMs then analyze reflection sequences to identify scene types, scene names, and objects. An N=10 study examines how capture conditions affect reflection fidelity, measures VLM detections, misclassifications, and hallucinations, and explores interaction scenarios such as steering-wheel detection for driver/passenger distinction.
AI.result: The study demonstrates that VLMs can extract some contextual information from smartphone-captured corneal reflections, despite their distortion and limited detail. Performance is sensitive to capture conditions, and the systems produce both recognition errors and hallucinations. The work also shows feasibility for interaction concepts, including identifying a steering wheel to infer whether a person is driving or riding as a passenger.
AI.conclusion: EyeQ establishes corneal reflection as a promising but imperfect modality for context-aware mobile interaction using a single face-facing camera. It broadens the role of the eye in HCI from gaze-estimation target to passive environmental mirror, while highlighting the need to address capture reliability, model errors, hallucinations, and privacy risks before practical deployment.

title: How Well Do Benchmarks Evaluate LLMs' Use for Personal Health Informatics?
summary: Benchmarking is a valuable technique for advancing the capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs), including in personal health informatics. There are growing efforts on benchmark creation for personal health data activities. However, it is unclear whether and how well these efforts align with needs and considerations of personal health informatics process. Addressing this need, we first analyzed 53,587 tasks across eight benchmarks related to personal health informatics and characterized the space of benchmark design. We then contrasted our observations of design choices with personal informatics theories and empirical knowledge. We find significant mismatches between existing benchmark design and domain guidelines and understanding. This lack of alignment limits the utility of the evidence current benchmarks offer about LLM capabilities. We use domain knowledge to highlight capabilities benchmarks should include and discuss opportunities our work enables for taking a human-centered and domain-driven approach to benchmark design.

AI.tldr: The paper systematically evaluates whether existing LLM benchmarks for personal health informatics reflect the field’s theories, empirical findings, and human-centered requirements. By analyzing 53,587 tasks from eight benchmarks, it identifies substantial design mismatches and argues for domain-driven benchmark development.
AI.motivation: Although benchmarking is increasingly used to assess LLMs in personal health informatics, it is unclear whether current benchmarks measure capabilities that matter for real personal informatics processes. Misalignment with domain knowledge may make benchmark results an unreliable indication of practical usefulness.
AI.method: The authors analyze 53,587 tasks across eight personal-health-informatics-related LLM benchmarks and characterize their design space. They then compare observed benchmark design choices with established personal informatics theories, guidelines, and empirical knowledge to identify areas of alignment and mismatch.
AI.result: The analysis reveals significant discrepancies between existing benchmark designs and the needs identified by personal informatics research. These mismatches concern which capabilities are assessed and how personal health activities are represented, limiting the interpretability and utility of current evidence about LLM capabilities.
AI.conclusion: Current benchmarks do not adequately capture important capabilities for personal health informatics. The paper advocates human-centered, domain-driven benchmark design and identifies opportunities for incorporating personal informatics knowledge into future evaluations.

title: Seeing Without Seeing: A Methodological Review of Visual Mental Imagery Reconstruction from Brain Activity
summary: Reconstructing visual mental imagery from brain activity differs from reconstructing perceived images. Imagery is generated top-down, its signal is weak, and the imagined content is never observed, so decoders are trained and scored against a proxy such as a cue or a seen exemplar. This criterion-guided methodological review of mainly non-invasive studies (fMRI, EEG, MEG) is narrative rather than systematic. We organise the field into a two-stage pipeline, two design axes and four method families, and formalise target-free evaluation, in which the proxy gap is a systematic bias rather than noise. A two-dimensional admissibility criterion crosses trial-level separability from working-memory maintenance with the memory source of the imagined content. Among the studies reviewed, every image-scored reconstruction concerns a recalled exemplar, none builds a scorable target for concept-generated content, and all come from fMRI, consistent with missing image-level targets in electrophysiological data. Published values for five decoders, compared under a common human forced-choice framing, show seen-to-imagined drops of 5.9 to 26.1 percentage points and a change in method ordering. We treat this as a diagnostic signal, not a controlled benchmark result, and specify a within-subject test for an altered neural code. Beyond this synthesis, we make two proposals. First, because frozen generative priors can produce photorealistic images weakly tied to neural signals, we combine existing null-signal controls into a normalised neural dependence with a within-category null, an unvalidated diagnostic quantity. Second, we propose a candidate ten-item reporting checklist with illustrative pass criteria. In an exploratory application to ten studies, none reports all items in a fully checkable form; this describes reporting practice, not study quality.

AI.tldr: A methodological review of non-invasive brain-imaging research on reconstructing visual mental imagery. It argues that imagery reconstruction is systematically harder to evaluate than perception reconstruction because the imagined target is unobserved and studies often score against imperfect proxies. The review organizes methods, identifies a proxy-induced evaluation bias, reports lower imagined-than-seen performance, and proposes diagnostics and a reporting checklist.
AI.motivation: Visual mental imagery is generated internally and top-down, producing weaker and potentially different neural signals from perception. Because the actual imagined image is unavailable as a direct ground truth, reconstruction studies rely on cues or seen exemplars, making it difficult to determine whether a decoder reconstructs imagery itself or merely matches a proxy. The paper addresses this methodological and evaluation gap.
AI.method: The authors conduct a criterion-guided, narrative review of mainly non-invasive fMRI, EEG, and MEG studies. They structure the literature as a two-stage reconstruction pipeline, two design axes, and four method families. They define a two-dimensional admissibility criterion based on trial-level separability from working-memory maintenance and on the memory source of the imagined content. They compare published decoder values using a common human forced-choice framing, formalize target-free evaluation as a systematic proxy gap, propose a within-subject test for altered neural coding, suggest a normalized neural-dependence measure with within-category null controls, and introduce a ten-item reporting checklist.
AI.result: All reviewed image-scored reconstructions involve recalled exemplars; none constructs a directly scorable image-level target for concept-generated imagery, and all such studies use fMRI. Across five decoders, imagined-image performance is 5.9–26.1 percentage points lower than seen-image performance, with a change in method ranking. In an exploratory assessment of ten studies, no study reports all checklist items in a fully checkable form. The proposed normalized neural-dependence measure remains unvalidated.
AI.conclusion: Evaluation of visual imagery reconstruction is currently constrained by missing or indirect targets, creating a systematic proxy bias rather than ordinary random noise. The field should distinguish recalled from concept-generated imagery, test for altered neural codes within subjects, use stronger null controls, and improve reporting transparency. The reported performance differences are diagnostic observations rather than controlled benchmark results, so they should not be interpreted as definitive evidence that one decoder is superior.

title: Where do we Jam? - The Impact of Real and Virtual XR Spaces on Musical Creativity, Co-Presence, Affect, and Flow
comment: Accepted at IEEE International Symposium on the Internet of Sound (IS2) 2026, 3rd International Workshop on the Musical Metaverse (IWMM)
summary: Extended Reality (XR) technologies can place musicians in virtual, mixed, or real environments during networked music performance (NMP). To examine how NMP applications in XR should be positioned on the reality-virtuality continuum, we conducted a laboratory study (N = 28) comparing a simulated NMP experience in Virtual Reality (VR) with one in Augmented Reality (AR). In both conditions, musicians saw their remote partners in real time as 3D point clouds rendered with an optimized Gaussian Splatting shader. While VR allowed participants to select and customize fully virtual 3D environments, AR showed a pass-through view of the laboratory environment. We measured creativity support, flow, involvement, co-presence, and affect, and complemented these data with qualitative interviews on participants' preferences and requirements for creative environments. Our results show that participants felt significantly more involved by the immersive XR experience in VR than in AR. Positive affect, flow, and creativity support were strongly correlated in both conditions, whereas involvement correlated with flow and creativity support only in VR. Qualitative findings showed substantial variation in participants' preferences for AR or VR and also regarding the design of creative virtual environments. Together, these findings suggest that the surrounding environment is a critical design dimension in networked Musical XR, shaping collaborative musical experiences beyond merely representing remote collaborators and mitigating communication latency. Future XR-mediated NMP systems should therefore treat the surrounding space as an integral component of the collaborative musical experience, rather than as a mere visual backdrop. At the same time, they should support experiences across a broad spectrum of the reality-virtuality continuum to accommodate highly individual user requirements.

AI.tldr: A laboratory comparison of VR- and AR-mediated networked music performance (N=28) found that VR produced greater involvement, while positive affect, flow, and creativity support were closely related in both settings. The study argues that the surrounding XR environment is a central component of collaborative musical experience and should be adaptable across the reality–virtuality continuum.
AI.motivation: The study addresses the limited understanding of how XR environments should be positioned on the reality–virtuality continuum for networked musical performance. It investigates whether the surrounding environment—fully virtual in VR versus real-world pass-through in AR—affects musicians’ creative and collaborative experiences beyond simply displaying remote performers and reducing perceived communication barriers.
AI.method: A laboratory study with 28 participants compared simulated networked music performance in VR and AR. In both conditions, remote musical partners were represented in real time as 3D point clouds using an optimized Gaussian Splatting shader. The VR condition allowed participants to select and customize fully virtual environments, whereas the AR condition displayed the physical laboratory through pass-through video. The researchers measured creativity support, flow, involvement, co-presence, and affect, and conducted qualitative interviews about environmental preferences and design requirements.
AI.result: Participants reported significantly greater involvement in VR than in AR. Positive affect, flow, and creativity support were strongly correlated in both conditions. Involvement was correlated with flow and creativity support only in VR. Interview findings revealed substantial individual differences in preferences for AR versus VR and in desired creative-environment designs.
AI.conclusion: The surrounding environment is a critical design dimension in networked Musical XR, influencing collaborative musical experience rather than serving merely as a visual backdrop. Future systems should treat environmental design as integral to musical collaboration and support multiple points across the reality–virtuality continuum to accommodate individual preferences and creative requirements.

title: BODYinTRANSIT-Lab: A Multimodal Dataset for Investigating Sensory-Driven Transformations in Body Perception and Affective Experiences
comment: 18 Pages, 6 Figures, 7 Tables. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Affective Computing
summary: Multimodal datasets that combine synchronised behavioural and physiological signals with subjective affective and body perception measures are still rare. This limits both the understanding of embodied experience and the development of computational models that infer subjective states from sensor data. We introduce BODYinTRANSIT-Lab, a multimodal dataset that addresses this gap by capturing affective, perceptual, and behavioural responses to the Footsteps Illusion. In this closed-loop paradigm, participants perform walking tasks while receiving real-time manipulated auditory feedback of their own footsteps intended to alter perceived body weight. The dataset comprises synchronised recordings from 101 participants recruited through systematic stratification by eating-disorder symptomatology and physical activity level. BODYinTRANSIT-Lab combines full-body kinematics with electromyography, electrocardiography, respiration, and electrodermal activity. Its annotations capture both immediate and post-trial experience, including within-trial perceived-weight ratings, post-trial assessments of body feelings and affective experience, 3D avatar body visualisations, and quantitative body maps. Psychological, behavioural, demographic, and social measures provide further information about factors that may influence individual responses. We provide a deep learning benchmark that uses walking kinematics to classify relative affective valence and perceived weight within subjects. On within-session, segment-level splits, the baseline model achieved mean balanced accuracies of 45.9% for affective valence and 44.5% for perceived weight. The BODYinTRANSIT-Lab dataset provides an experimentally controlled resource for cognitive neuroscience and affective computing research, with potential applications in affect-aware interactive systems, health and well-being technologies, and creative embodied experiences.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces BODYinTRANSIT-Lab, a multimodal dataset designed to study how manipulated auditory feedback during walking affects perceived body weight, affective experience, and behaviour. It combines synchronized physiological, kinematic, subjective, and demographic data from 101 participants and demonstrates an initial deep-learning benchmark for predicting affective valence and perceived weight from walking kinematics.
AI.motivation: Existing datasets rarely synchronize behavioural and physiological signals with subjective measures of affect and body perception. This limits research on embodied experience and the development of computational models that infer subjective states from sensor data. The study addresses this gap by creating a controlled dataset based on the Footsteps Illusion, in which auditory feedback is manipulated to influence perceived body weight during walking.
AI.method: The authors collected data from 101 systematically stratified participants varying in eating-disorder symptomatology and physical activity level. Participants performed walking tasks in a closed-loop setup while hearing real-time manipulated feedback of their own footsteps. The dataset includes full-body kinematics, electromyography, electrocardiography, respiration, electrodermal activity, within-trial perceived-weight ratings, post-trial body and affect ratings, 3D avatar body visualizations, quantitative body maps, and psychological, behavioural, demographic, and social measures. As a benchmark, a deep-learning model used walking-kinematic segments to classify relative affective valence and perceived weight within participants.
AI.result: The dataset provides synchronized multimodal recordings and annotations covering immediate and retrospective subjective experience. In the baseline benchmark, within-session segment-level splits produced mean balanced accuracies of 45.9% for affective valence and 44.5% for perceived weight. These results indicate that walking kinematics contain some information about the targeted subjective states, although performance remains modest.
AI.conclusion: BODYinTRANSIT-Lab offers a controlled and information-rich resource for studying embodied perception, affect, and physiological responses. It supports cognitive neuroscience and affective-computing research and may enable future affect-aware interactive systems, health and well-being technologies, and creative embodied applications. The benchmark also establishes a baseline for developing more accurate subject-state inference models.

title: CUVE: Making Supervised Classification more Accessible through Visualization
summary: We present CUVE, an interface that enables people to build classifiers by generating visualizations that are interpretable by both humans and learning algorithms (the Visualization as Intermediate Representation approach). This UI enables users to create supervised classifiers and to visually investigate how to improve them and how they carry out their function. A preliminary study investigates the usability of our prototype and compares it with a traditional text-based programming interface.

AI.tldr: The paper presents CUVE, a visual programming interface for building and inspecting supervised classifiers by using visualizations as an intermediate representation understandable to both humans and machine-learning algorithms.
AI.motivation: Traditional text-based programming makes it difficult for non-experts to construct classifiers and understand how those classifiers operate or how to improve them. CUVE is motivated by the need for a more interpretable and interactive approach to classifier creation and analysis.
AI.method: The authors develop a prototype interface in which users generate visual representations that are processed as classifier specifications. The system supports supervised-classifier construction, visual investigation of classifier behavior, and iterative improvement. A preliminary user study evaluates prototype usability and compares CUVE with a conventional text-based programming interface.
AI.result: The abstract reports that a preliminary study was conducted, but it does not provide specific quantitative findings. It indicates that the study assessed usability and comparative performance against text-based programming, without stating the exact outcomes.
AI.conclusion: CUVE demonstrates the potential of Visualization as Intermediate Representation for making classifier development more accessible and interpretable. The preliminary evaluation provides initial evidence for its usability, although stronger conclusions require detailed results and broader evaluation.

title: Uneven Self-Reported AI Use: An Embedded Case Study Across Eleven Teams in a Software Organization
summary: This paper presents a descriptive, embedded single-case study examining self-reported AI use within a software organization. The study draws on 98 structured interview records collected across 11 teams, using ten standardized team-level instruments (n = 65) and one instrument with distinct response anchors (n = 33). Among respondents assessed using standardized instruments, 36 of 65 (55.4%) reported AI-use frequency scores of 4 or 5 on a five-point scale. Team-level proportions varied from 20.0% (1/5) to 71.4% (5/7). A record-level cross-tabulation revealed limited awareness or understanding of organizational AI policies across both frequency groups: 86.1% (31/36) of respondents scoring 4-5 and 96.6% (28/29) of those scoring 0-3 reported either no policy awareness or uncertainty about policy details. In the group assessed using the distinct instrument, 31 of 33 respondents (93.9%) scored 4 or 5. Although the pooled proportion reached 68.4% (67/98), differences in response anchors limit direct comparability, making the standardized-instrument results the primary analytical reference. Interviewer-recorded observations provide qualitative context on reported practices and constraints but do not support estimates of their prevalence or causal explanations for differences in AI-use frequency. The findings characterize AI-use patterns and policy awareness within the interviewed sample, without supporting inferences about organization-wide adoption, policy compliance, or the effectiveness of AI use. The study contributes an empirically grounded organizational case and an explicit account of the methodological boundaries of cross-team comparisons using heterogeneous interview instruments.

AI.tldr: A descriptive embedded single-case study analyzes self-reported AI-use frequency and awareness of organizational AI policies across 98 interview records from 11 software-organization teams. Among the 65 respondents assessed with comparable instruments, 55.4% reported high AI-use frequency (scores 4–5), while 86.1% of high-frequency and 96.6% of lower-frequency respondents lacked policy awareness or were uncertain about policy details. A separate 33-person instrument produced substantially higher scores but is not directly comparable. The study describes the interviewed sample only and does not establish organization-wide adoption, compliance, causality, or effectiveness.
AI.motivation: The study is motivated by the need to empirically characterize how frequently employees report using AI in a software organization and how this use relates to awareness of organizational AI policies. It also addresses a methodological concern: cross-team comparisons can be misleading when interview instruments use different response anchors. The paper therefore emphasizes transparent description and explicit limits on generalization.
AI.method: The researchers conducted a descriptive, embedded single-case study using 98 structured interview records from 11 teams. Ten team-level instruments used standardized response anchors and yielded 65 observations; one instrument used different anchors and yielded 33 observations. AI-use frequency was summarized on a five-point scale, with scores of 4–5 treated as high frequency. A record-level cross-tabulation compared AI-use-frequency groups with reported awareness or understanding of organizational AI policies. Interviewer-recorded observations were used as qualitative context, not for prevalence estimation or causal analysis. Because of measurement heterogeneity, the standardized-instrument subset served as the primary analytical basis.
AI.result: In the standardized subset, 36 of 65 respondents (55.4%) reported high AI-use frequency, with team-level proportions ranging from 20.0% to 71.4%. Policy awareness was limited in both frequency groups: 31 of 36 high-frequency respondents (86.1%) and 28 of 29 lower-frequency respondents (96.6%) reported no awareness or uncertainty about policy details. The distinct-instrument group showed 31 of 33 high scores (93.9%), but its results are not directly comparable. The pooled estimate of 67 of 98 (68.4%) is therefore treated cautiously. Qualitative observations add contextual detail but do not establish prevalence or explain between-team differences.
AI.conclusion: The study documents substantial self-reported AI use among interviewed employees, alongside generally limited awareness or understanding of organizational AI policies. However, the evidence supports only a bounded description of this case and sample. It cannot justify claims about organization-wide adoption, policy compliance, causal relationships between policy awareness and AI use, or the effectiveness of AI use. Its main contribution is the empirical case description and the careful demonstration that heterogeneous measurement instruments constrain cross-team and pooled comparisons.

title: Lilo: A Multi-Agent Conversational Sandbox for Children's Digital Communication
summary: Children's peer conflicts increasingly play out in group chats, where tone and timing are stripped away, and a hurtful message is easier to send than to say aloud. We present Lilo, a multi-agent conversational system that lets children practice such conversations, so they are better prepared when they encounter them in real digital communication. In Lilo, the child joins two AI-driven peers mid-argument, coached by a mentor character, also named Lilo, through a Stop-Think-Act traffic light. Through an exploratory study with 28 children (aged 9-11), we examine how children engage with Lilo's simulated peer conflict and the mentor's traffic-light interventions. The study included an intervention with Lilo, surveys before and after the intervention, and exit interviews. Participants reported significantly higher self-efficacy for coping with unpleasant messages after their interaction with Lilo. They felt safe experimenting, knowing nothing they wrote would be held against them.

AI.tldr: The paper presents Lilo, a multi-agent conversational system that helps children practice responding to peer conflicts in group chats. In an exploratory study with 28 children aged 9–11, participants practiced conflict scenarios with AI peers and received Stop–Think–Act guidance from a mentor character. Children reported significantly greater self-efficacy in coping with unpleasant messages after the intervention and felt safe experimenting in the simulated environment.
AI.motivation: Children increasingly encounter peer conflict through digital group chats, where missing tone and timing can make hurtful communication easier and more difficult to interpret or manage. Existing preparation may not provide a safe, interactive way for children to rehearse responses. The study therefore investigates whether a conversational simulation can support children’s confidence and readiness in these situations.
AI.method: The authors developed Lilo, a multi-agent conversational system in which a child enters an ongoing argument between two AI-driven peers. A mentor character provides Stop–Think–Act traffic-light interventions during the interaction. The exploratory study involved 28 children aged 9–11 and used a Lilo intervention, pre- and post-intervention surveys, and exit interviews. The design appears to assess changes in self-efficacy and children’s experiences of the simulated conflict and mentoring support.
AI.result: After interacting with Lilo, participants reported significantly higher self-efficacy for coping with unpleasant messages. They also described the environment as safe for experimentation because their responses would not have real-world consequences. The abstract does not report detailed quantitative effect sizes, comparison groups, or specific findings from the interviews.
AI.conclusion: Lilo shows preliminary promise as a safe, interactive tool for helping children rehearse responses to peer conflict in digital communication. The findings suggest that simulated practice combined with structured Stop–Think–Act guidance can improve perceived coping confidence. Because the study is exploratory and small, further research is needed to test behavioral transfer to real-world group chats, long-term effects, and effectiveness against alternative interventions.

title: Ninety-Six Ways to Measure a Scribe: Fragmented Evaluation of Ambient Scribes in Healthcare
summary: Ambient artificial intelligence (AI) scribes have moved rapidly from experimental pilots to enterprise-wide deployment across health systems, promising reduced documentation burden and improved clinician experience. While research evaluating these tools has expanded quickly, there are no agreed-upon protocols or standardized metrics for assessing their performance, making it difficult to compare findings or cumulatively synthesize evidence across studies. Across 54 recent evaluation studies, we identify ten evaluation dimensions and 40 distinct metrics, operationalized in 96 different ways-35 of them (36%) used by only a single study. Assessment is dominated by documentation efficiency and time, measured in 44 of 54 studies. The other dimensions appear at broadly similar rates (16-24 studies each), and safety and clinical outcome least consistently of all. Ripple effects on the broader care system, such as impact on patients' care outcomes, redistribution of work, changes in billing and coding intensity, and downstream use of notes by other clinicians are rarely assessed. Moreover, the metrics used rely heavily on self-report and are fragmented and inconsistently operationalized, which limits comparability and hinders synthesis across studies. As an effort to support more rigorous and cumulative evaluation, in this paper we review the study designs, data sources, and metrics commonly used to evaluate ambient AI scribes in healthcare settings, discuss the limitations of current evaluation practice, and argue for a more holistic approach grounded in a standardized, multi-dimensional set of metrics.

AI.tldr: This paper reviews 54 studies evaluating ambient AI scribes in healthcare and finds substantial fragmentation in evaluation methods: ten dimensions and 40 metrics were measured in 96 inconsistent ways, with heavy emphasis on documentation efficiency and limited assessment of safety, clinical outcomes, and broader system effects. It proposes standardized, multidimensional evaluation protocols and metrics to improve comparability and evidence synthesis.
AI.motivation: Ambient AI scribes are being deployed rapidly across health systems, but evaluations lack agreed-upon protocols, standardized metrics, and consistent operational definitions. This prevents meaningful comparison across studies and limits cumulative evidence about effectiveness, safety, clinician experience, and system-level consequences.
AI.method: The paper conducts a review of 54 recent evaluation studies of ambient AI scribes in healthcare. It categorizes the studies by design, data sources, evaluation dimensions, and metrics, identifying ten dimensions, 40 distinct metrics, and 96 operationalizations. It also examines how frequently each dimension is assessed and the extent to which measures rely on self-report or address broader care-system effects.
AI.result: Evaluation is dominated by documentation efficiency and time, assessed in 44 of 54 studies. Other dimensions appear in 16–24 studies, while safety and clinical outcomes are assessed least consistently. Thirty-five of the 96 metric operationalizations are used by only one study. Measures rely heavily on self-report, and ripple effects—such as patient outcomes, work redistribution, billing and coding changes, and downstream use of notes—are rarely evaluated.
AI.conclusion: Current evidence on ambient AI scribes is difficult to compare or synthesize because evaluation practices are fragmented, inconsistently operationalized, and overly focused on efficiency. The paper calls for a holistic, standardized, multidimensional evaluation framework that includes documentation, clinician, patient, safety, clinical, and broader health-system outcomes.

title: AI Isn't Getting Dumber, We're Getting Pickier: Rising Standards in Human Evaluation of Large Language Models
summary: Users often complain that AI assistants such as ChatGPT are getting worse. Some versions do change, but human evaluation leaves a second possibility untested: the people judging may change. We separate the two on Chatbot Arena, a public platform where people compare answers from two anonymous large language models (LLMs) and pick the better one or say both are bad. We study 1,260,967 blind votes cast from May 2023 to August 2024 on pairs of models whose versions are fixed: dated vendor snapshots and models with fixed open weights. For the same pair of unchanged models, the share of votes saying "both are bad" rises by 1.71 percentage points a month on a mean of 17.1%, and by 1.91 points a month in 2024. In fourteen pairs observed often in both 2023 and 2024, it rose in every one, from 15.5% to 23.3%. The ranking does not trend: in 2024, the stronger model's share of decisive votes is flat. The rise holds within the same voter and on the same pair, and across arrival cohorts from their first recorded vote. It holds with prompt controls, in every major language, for dated vendor snapshots, open-weight models and models with stable answer length, and between interface changes. The drift is shared across models: month effects estimated from other models' pairs remove it from each model's own pairs. Platform-wide, the average model would be expected to score 78% against the 2023 average, yet the share of "both are bad" votes ended near where it began. The pattern fits a standard that follows the category's progress, so a product that stands still is judged as declining. Absolute verdicts on AI drifted while relative comparisons held steady, an evaluation drift that matters for LLM leaderboards and for the human feedback used to train models.

AI.tldr: The paper finds that users increasingly judge unchanged LLMs as jointly poor over time, even though relative model rankings remain stable. This suggests evaluation drift: user standards rise as the overall AI category improves.
AI.motivation: The study addresses widespread reports that AI assistants are getting worse. Such reports may reflect actual model degradation, changes in the evaluated models, or changes in user expectations and judging behavior. The paper isolates evaluator changes by analyzing votes on fixed model versions in Chatbot Arena.
AI.method: The authors analyze 1,260,967 blind pairwise votes collected from May 2023 to August 2024. They examine unchanged dated vendor snapshots and fixed open-weight models, measuring trends in the frequency of “both are bad” judgments and in relative model preferences. Robustness checks control for voter identity, arrival cohort, prompt characteristics, language, model type, answer length, interface changes, and model-pair effects. They also estimate shared month effects across model pairs to test whether the drift is platform-wide.
AI.result: For unchanged model pairs, “both are bad” votes increased by 1.71 percentage points per month from a baseline of 17.1%, and by 1.91 points per month in 2024. Across 14 repeatedly observed pairs, the rate rose from 15.5% in 2023 to 23.3% in 2024. In contrast, the stronger model’s share of decisive votes remained stable, indicating that relative rankings did not systematically deteriorate. The pattern persisted across voters, cohorts, languages, model classes, prompt controls, and other robustness checks. Cross-model month effects largely explained the increase, supporting a common platform-wide source. The average model would score approximately 78% against the 2023 average, suggesting overall capability growth despite increasing negative absolute judgments.
AI.conclusion: The findings support evaluation drift rather than broad model degradation: as the LLM category improves, users adopt higher standards, causing unchanged systems to receive more “both are bad” judgments. Relative comparisons remain comparatively stable, while absolute evaluations become harsher. This has implications for interpreting LLM leaderboards, monitoring perceived quality, and using human feedback to train models, because time-dependent changes in evaluator standards can confound apparent performance trends.

title: Evaluating Tactile Encoding Strategies for Communicating 3-D Shape
summary: Two-dimensional haptic displays, such as programmable pin arrays and vibrotactile or friction-modulating touchscreens, enable tactile communication of complex shapes in a low-profile form factor. However, many shapes of interest, including CAD models, three-dimensional graphs, and map topographies, are inherently three-dimensional. This work investigates two methods for encoding 3-D information using a 2-D tactile display: (1) a single tactile height map providing coarse but quantifiable depth cues, and (2) a series of binary layers communicating sequential slices of a 3-D model, supporting more complex geometries such as overhangs and cavities. We further compare performance across two display types--a friction-modulating display and a pin array--to examine how the level of haptic abstraction affects users' ability to decode discrete 3-D information. A user study demonstrates that participants were able to effectively complete a 3-D assembly task using both strategies, achieving high accuracy across all display types. While the pin array supported faster task completion and higher-rated--though not statistically significant--user experience than the friction-modulating display for the binary-layer task, these differences did not translate to significant differences in overall usability (i.e., reassembly accuracy success). Together, these results identify design trade-offs and inform development of future surface haptic displays that support the communication and interpretation of discrete 3-D information in tactile graphics.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates two ways to communicate three-dimensional geometry through two-dimensional tactile displays: a continuous height map and sequential binary slices. A user study using both a friction-modulating surface and a pin array found high assembly accuracy for all conditions. The pin array enabled faster performance for the binary-layer method, but display type did not significantly affect overall usability.
AI.motivation: Many tactile displays are physically two-dimensional, whereas important information sources—such as CAD models, 3-D graphs, and terrain maps—are inherently three-dimensional. Existing tactile representations may not adequately convey overhangs, cavities, and other complex geometry. The paper therefore investigates practical encoding strategies and examines whether the type of haptic display influences users’ ability to interpret discrete 3-D information.
AI.method: The study compares two encoding strategies on 2-D tactile displays: (1) a single tactile height map that conveys depth through surface elevation, and (2) sequential binary layers that represent slices of a 3-D object and can encode overhangs and cavities. Both methods are evaluated on two display technologies: a friction-modulating touchscreen and a programmable pin array. Participants complete a 3-D assembly task, with performance assessed primarily through reassembly accuracy, alongside task completion time and subjective user-experience/usability ratings.
AI.result: Participants achieved high accuracy across both encoding strategies and both display types, demonstrating that 2-D tactile displays can effectively communicate discrete 3-D structure. For the binary-layer condition, the pin array produced faster task completion and higher subjective experience ratings than the friction-modulating display, although the rating difference was not statistically significant. These performance differences did not yield a significant difference in overall usability as measured by reassembly accuracy success.
AI.conclusion: Both height-map and binary-layer representations are viable for communicating 3-D information through 2-D tactile interfaces. Binary layers offer greater representational flexibility for complex geometries, while pin arrays may provide efficiency advantages for sequential-slice interaction. However, the lack of significant accuracy or overall usability differences indicates that display technology and encoding strategy involve trade-offs rather than a single universally superior solution. The findings provide design guidance for future tactile graphics and surface-haptic systems.

title: Demonstration of MANA: Multi-perspective Alignment of NPC Agents
summary: We present MANA (Multi-perspective Alignment of NPC Agents), an interactive approach for authoring NPC behavior through embodied demonstration. We show MANA in the context of Minecraft, where a developer aligns NPCs while playing the game itself. Activating MANA lets the developer dynamically switch into the point of view (POV) of any character and demonstrate, in-situ, how it would act given the surrounding context, through both movement and dialogue. MANA then distills each demonstration into a generalized policy that maps in-game context to actions. Finally, once the developer switches to another NPC or exits MANA mode, this generalized policy drives the NPC on its own. We demonstrate MANA by aligning two initially generic Minecraft NPCs: Fletcher and Farmer to act aggressively and cowardly, respectively. After roughly 2 minutes of in-game play, each character exhibits consistent and believable behaviors across new, unseen scenarios.

AI.tldr: MANA is an interactive system for authoring believable Minecraft NPC behavior through embodied, in-game demonstrations. Developers switch into an NPC’s viewpoint, demonstrate movement and dialogue, and the system generalizes these examples into a policy that autonomously controls the NPC in new situations.
AI.motivation: Authoring NPC behavior typically requires separate programming or scripting workflows and can be difficult to ground in the game’s immediate context. The paper addresses the need for a more natural, interactive, and expressive way for developers to specify character behavior while directly experiencing the game world.
AI.method: MANA (Multi-perspective Alignment of NPC Agents) allows a developer to activate an NPC-specific mode, assume the point of view of any character, and demonstrate desired behavior through embodied actions, including movement and dialogue. The system converts each demonstration into a generalized policy mapping in-game context to actions. The policy is then used to control the NPC after the developer switches to another character or leaves the authoring mode. The approach is demonstrated in Minecraft by aligning two initially generic NPCs, Fletcher and Farmer, with aggressive and cowardly behavioral styles.
AI.result: After approximately two minutes of in-game interaction, the two NPCs displayed consistent and believable behavior in new, unseen scenarios. The demonstration suggests that MANA can efficiently transfer developer-intended behavioral styles from a small amount of interactive supervision to autonomous NPC control.
AI.conclusion: MANA provides an interactive, embodied approach to NPC behavior authoring that integrates demonstration directly into gameplay. The reported Minecraft example indicates that developers can quickly create coherent character behaviors without manually specifying every situation, although the abstract does not provide quantitative evaluations, comparisons with alternative methods, or details about the policy-learning algorithm.
